prompt.context: H Hotel is a hotel company operating in two segments: Business Hotels and Vacation Hotels. The client is the leader in the Business Hotel segment and an average player in the Vacation Hotel segment. The overall hotel market is stable.
prompt.question: H Hotel is considering raising its daily room rate from $160 to $180. Should they do it?

clarifying_info.q: What segment is H Hotel focused on?
clarifying_info.a: The client has decided to focus on the Business Hotel unit.
H Hotel has contracts with large corporations; business travelers are the end users but the corporations are the paying customers.

clarifying_info.q: What is the corporate travel expense cap?
clarifying_info.a: The corporate travel expense cap is $240 per night.

clarifying_info.q: Is the $180 price competitive vs. competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, $180 is still competitive compared to H Hotel's competitors.
Cost savings have largely been exhausted — the company already outsourced cleaning services, went through a major layoff cutting staff by half, and their restaurant and bar are operating efficiently.

clarifying_info.q: What are the two hotel industry segments?
clarifying_info.a: Business hotels (located in metropolitan centers, smaller, business-service equipped, flexible booking) and vacation hotels (touristy/scenic areas, wider price range, more demand fluctuation).

framework: Industry overview: characterize the hotel industry segments (business vs. vacation) and H Hotel's competitive position in each

Internal company analysis: understand why H Hotel focuses on Business Hotels and why they want to raise prices (profitability); assess Profit = Revenue – Cost and whether cost or revenue levers are more promising
External consumer analysis: assess impact on end users (business travelers) and customers (corporations) — price sensitivity, switching triggers, and expense caps
Competitive analysis: evaluate whether the new price remains competitive and whether H Hotel's advantages are defensible
Demand growth: identify actions H Hotel can take to increase occupancy (quantity) after the price increase
Recommendation: synthesize whether to raise the price and what to do alongside it

questions.prompt: Why did H Hotel decide to focus on the Business Hotel segment?
questions.guidance: Strong answers cover: (1) Location advantage — as segment leader H Hotel has already secured prime city-center locations; limited space makes these hard to replicate. (2) Steady revenue stream — corporate contracts make demand predictable, driving higher occupancy rates and enabling fixed pricing. (3) Lower maintenance cost — smaller properties with fewer recreational facilities are cheaper to run.

questions.prompt: From an internal view, why does H Hotel want to raise the price, and does it make sense?
questions.guidance: The candidate should build a profit equation: Profit = Revenue – Cost = (Price × Quantity) – (Fixed Cost + Variable Cost). Key insight: cost-saving options are exhausted (cleaning outsourced, staff halved, F&B efficient). Therefore, the only path to profit improvement is top-line growth — either higher price or higher occupancy. Raising price from $160 to $180 is a direct lever.

math.setup: Profit = Price × Occupancy – (Fixed Cost + Variable Cost). Cost levers exhausted; revenue lever = price increase of $20/room/night.
steps: Revenue per room increases by $20 if occupancy holds constant
Focus shifts to whether demand (occupancy) will fall when price rises
math.answer: If occupancy is maintained, the $20 price increase flows directly to profit improvement.

questions.prompt: How will the price increase impact consumer behavior — both end users (travelers) and customers (corporations)?
questions.guidance: Must distinguish two stakeholder types. End users (travelers): impact is limited because they don't pay out of pocket; they will stay at H Hotel as long as service, flexibility, and location remain unchanged. Customers (corporations): will only leave if (1) price becomes uncompetitive vs. rivals — at $180 it is still competitive, (2) price exceeds the corporate travel expense cap of $240 — $180 is well below, or (3) no extra benefits accompany the price increase — H Hotel can offer better services and business-friendly facilities.

questions.prompt: What can H Hotel do to increase demand from end users (travelers) after the price increase?
questions.guidance: Product differentiation: improve convenience (e.g., dedicated transportation, prime locations in emerging city areas); enhance business friendliness (in-room fax/printer); upgrade rooms. Service differentiation: personalized experience by tracking each traveler's preferences, customizing room setup. Loyalty/lock-in: traveler-specific promotions such as free gifts (shopping coupons), cross-promotions between Business and Vacation Hotels (e.g., free vacation-hotel stay for family trips), to reduce churn among travelers who have multiple hotel options.

brainstorming.prompt: What actions can H Hotel take to increase demand from end users (business travelers) to support the price increase?

categories.name: Product Improvements
ideas: Provide in-room fax, printer, and high-speed internet
Secure locations in the hottest emerging business districts
Offer dedicated transportation (airport shuttles, car service)

categories.name: Service & Personalization
ideas: Track individual traveler preferences and pre-set rooms accordingly
Assign dedicated relationship managers to frequent travelers
Offer 24/7 concierge tailored to business needs

categories.name: Loyalty & Lock-in
ideas: Cross-promotion: free vacation hotel stay for family trips
Points or reward program tied to the individual traveler, not just the corporation
Priority booking windows for frequent guests

recommendation: Yes, H Hotel should raise its daily room rate from $160 to $180.

H Hotel holds competitive advantages — superior city-center locations, strong service, and long-term corporate relationships — that justify the premium. At $180 the price remains far below the corporate expense cap of $240 and is still competitive versus rivals.
risks: If occupancy falls significantly, the revenue gain from the higher price could be offset by lost room-nights
Corporate clients could renegotiate contracts at renewal if they perceive insufficient value for the higher rate
Competitors could respond aggressively on price or service to capture H Hotel's corporate accounts
next_steps: Introduce product and service enhancements (better business facilities, personalized service) to justify the higher rate and reduce churn risk
Launch traveler-specific loyalty programs to lock in end users who have discretion over hotel choice
Monitor occupancy rates closely after the price change and be prepared to adjust quickly if demand softens
